findings.title: Catch-all diagnostic filter hides the real rule and also drops location-less diagnostics for source types
findings.body:
The fix wraps every `reportDiagnostic` call in `ReportIfLocatedInCompilation`, which drops any diagnostic unless `Location.IsInSource && compilation.ContainsSyntaxTree(...)`. The real rule ("don't analyse members of types defined in another assembly") is never written down. It has to be inferred from where diagnostics happen to land, and it now applies to every diagnostic TypeCollector emits, not just the issue #2283 path.

The rule also catches more than it should. Many existing call sites build locations with `?.FirstOrDefault()?...GetLocation()` and can produce `Location.None`. One example is `MessageFormatterMustBeMessagePackFormatter` at line 693–695: when the `[MessagePackFormatter]` attribute sits on a type from metadata, `ApplicationSyntaxReference` is null. That diagnostic used to reach the consumer as a location-less warning. Now it is silently discarded. The remark at lines 1442–1445 says analyzers "are not permitted" to report against a non-existent location. That is wrong for `Location.None`, which Roslyn accepts. Roslyn only rejects source locations in syntax trees outside the compilation.

The policy is also applied unevenly. The constructor (line 248) still calls the raw `reportAnalyzerDiagnostic`. And two call sites were separately patched from `DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0]` to null-safe forms (lines 985, 1077). So the fix is spread across three mechanisms: a wrapper, per-site null guards, and a bypass.

The simpler fix is to decide at the type boundary. `CollectCore` already has an `IsInMetadata` gate (line 367) for non-generic types. In `CollectGeneric`/`GetObjectInfo`, suppress diagnostics when `formattedType.OriginalDefinition` is not declared in `this.compilation.Assembly`, for example by passing a `reportDiagnostic` that is null for foreign types. The member-level null guards and the global filter then become unnecessary, and source types keep their current behaviour.
findings.reason: A global, location-based filter in a shared reporting path silently suppresses diagnostics beyond the issue's scope and makes the reporting policy hard to reason about. This code is a source generator and analyzer, so the effect reaches every consumer's build.
findings.fix: Replace the global wrapper with an explicit boundary. When the type whose members are being analysed (formattedType.OriginalDefinition) does not belong to this.compilation.Assembly, run GetObjectInfo with diagnostics disabled. Keep at most a ContainsSyntaxTree guard (not IsInSource) as a safety net. Then revert the per-site location rewrites, or keep them only as crash guards.

evidence.detail: TypeCollector.cs:239 wraps reportDiagnostic. Lines 1440–1452 define ReportIfLocatedInCompilation, which requires IsInSource (this drops Location.None). Line 693–695 can report with a null location for a metadata type's formatter attribute. Line 248 bypasses the wrapper. Line 367 shows the existing IsInMetadata boundary check. The generator path passes reportAnalyzerDiagnostic: null (MessagePackGenerator.cs:47), so the filter only affects the analyzer.
supporting: Roslyn rejects only source locations whose tree is outside the compilation (the analyzer-crash pattern in dotnet/runtime#109352, fixed with Compilation.ContainsSyntaxTree). Location.None is allowed.

verdict.note: Not run: no container was available (executor capacity errors on every checkout), so I could not test whether the ReportIfLocatedInCompilation filter drops Location.None diagnostics.

findings.title: Changed reporting branches lack tests; helper hand-builds a second compilation pipeline
findings.body:
The three new tests only check the happy path, where nothing is reported. Two altered behaviours have no test that would fail if they broke.

First, the new `GetPropertyIdentifierLocation` path for `BothStringAndIntKeyAreNull` (line 985) is never exercised by a metadata property with a null key.

Second, nothing pins down what the filter now drops. No test shows that a source-declared problem is still reported when the type is reached through a metadata generic. No test shows that a location-less diagnostic (for example an invalid formatter attribute on a referenced type) is now suppressed on purpose.

`RunWithMetadataReferenceAsync` also runs the generator twice. The first run uses VerifyCS with `SkipGeneratedSourcesCheck`. The second builds a separate `CSharpCompilation` with hard-coded `ReferenceAssemblies.Net.Net80` and its own `CSharpGeneratorDriver`, just to check a hint name. That duplicates the verifier's job and can drift from the harness's reference set.
findings.reason: Tests should fail when a changed condition flips. Here, removing the IsInSource check, or reverting line 985, would leave every new test green except the crash case.
findings.fix: Add one analyzer test with a source type that has a real MsgPack004 problem and a member of a metadata generic, and assert the source diagnostic is still reported. Add one test that pins down the intended handling of location-less diagnostics. Assert the generated resolver through the verifier's GeneratedSources, not through a second hand-built driver run.

evidence.detail: GenericsFormatterTests.cs patch lines 15–200: the three tests all expect zero diagnostics. None uses Key with a null value or an invalid formatter attribute on a metadata type. The helper at patch lines 149–175 runs VerifyCS and then a manual CSharpGeneratorDriver over a separately built compilation that pins Net80.

star.situation: Using a closed generic type from a referenced assembly (for example a generic struct or record struct) as a member of a [MessagePackObject] type could crash the MessagePack analyzer or generator. The cause was code that indexed DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0] and reported diagnostics against symbols that have no source (issue #2283).
star.task: The pull request sets out to stop the crash and to keep diagnostics about referenced-assembly members out of the consuming project.
star.action: TypeCollector now routes every analyzer diagnostic through ReportIfLocatedInCompilation, which drops any diagnostic whose location is not a source location in the current compilation. Two member-diagnostic locations are made null-safe, and README plus MsgPack004.md document the new rule.
star.result: Consumers can use referenced-assembly closed generics without AD0001 or CS8785, and no longer see diagnostics about those types' members. The pull request backs this with three new metadata-reference tests that expect zero diagnostics and a generated resolver.

verdict.summary: I found no blockers, but nothing was built or run: CI was absent and every shell call hit a busy executor. Two medium findings. (1) The fix is a catch-all location filter in the shared reporting path. It also drops Location.None diagnostics for cases outside the issue, such as an invalid formatter attribute on a referenced type. Its remark wrongly says analyzers cannot report location-less diagnostics, and the constructor bypasses it. The cleaner fix is a type-boundary rule: suppress diagnostics when the analysed type is not declared in this compilation, matching the existing IsInMetadata gate in CollectCore. (2) The new tests cover only the zero-diagnostic happy path. They would not fail if the IsInSource check or the line 985 location change were reverted, and the helper builds a second compilation and driver with Net80 hard-coded. The file was already over 1,000 lines at base, so the size threshold does not apply. The verifier also ran nothing (executor capacity) and reproduced neither finding. The dotnet-ci scanner failure (CS0117 in MessagePack.GeneratedCode.Tests/CompositeResolverTests.cs) is in a file this PR does not touch; I did not confirm its cause. dotnet-format reported no diagnostics.

checks.requirement: Issue #2283 (Missing .meta files cause Unity to reject the MessagePack package): every tracked asset file and folder inside each Unity package (folder with package.json under src/MessagePack.UnityClient) must have a matching tracked .meta file, and .meta GUIDs must be unique.
checks.content:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Blind check for MessagePack-CSharp #2283: Unity rejects packages whose assets lack .meta files.
# Usage: bash tests/blind-checks/unity-meta-check.sh   (run from repo root). Exit 0 = pass.
set -u
cd "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
fail=0
mapfile -t pkgs < <(git ls-files 'src/MessagePack.UnityClient/**/package.json' | xargs -r -n1 dirname | sort -u)
if [ ${#pkgs[@]} -eq 0 ]; then echo 'FAIL: no Unity package.json found'; exit 2; fi
tracked=$(mktemp)
git ls-files > "$tracked"
# include symlinked dirs' contents as seen on disk too
is_ignored() {
  # Unity ignores names starting with '.' or ending with '~', and cvs/tmp files
  local p="$1" part
  IFS='/' read -ra parts <<< "$p"
  for part in "${parts[@]}"; do
    case "$part" in .*|*~|cvs|*.tmp) return 0;; esac
  done
  return 1
}
missing=0; checked=0
for pkg in "${pkgs[@]}"; do
  echo "Package root: $pkg"
  # all files on disk (following symlinks) under package root
  while IFS= read -r f; do
    rel="${f#$pkg/}"
    is_ignored "$rel" && continue
    case "$f" in *.meta) continue;; esac
    checked=$((checked+1))
    if [ ! -f "$f.meta" ]; then echo "MISSING META (disk): $f"; missing=$((missing+1)); continue; fi
    if ! grep -qxF "$f.meta" "$tracked"; then
      # file may be reached through a symlinked directory; only require tracking when the asset itself is tracked
      if grep -qxF "$f" "$tracked"; then echo "META NOT TRACKED: $f.meta"; missing=$((missing+1)); fi
    fi
  done < <(find -L "$pkg" -mindepth 1 \( -type f -o -type d \) | sort)
  # dangling metas
  while IFS= read -r m; do
    base="${m%.meta}"
    if [ ! -e "$base" ]; then echo "DANGLING META: $m"; fi
  done < <(find -L "$pkg" -name '*.meta' -type f | sort)
  # duplicate guids
  dups=$(find -L "$pkg" -name '*.meta' -type f -exec grep -h '^guid:' {} + | sort | uniq -d)
  if [ -n "$dups" ]; then echo "DUPLICATE GUIDS: $dups"; fail=1; fi
done
rm -f "$tracked"
echo "checked=$checked missing=$missing"
if [ $missing -ne 0 ] || [ $fail -ne 0 ]; then echo FAIL; exit 1; fi
echo PASS
